strengths: By using the ECG specific information such as R peaks and the spectogram of signals, this paper seeks to reconstruct the original ECG more than other baseline methods.
The development of robust methodologies for analyzing single-lead ECG is necessary in this field.
The paper is well written, and easy to read.
The proposed method is interesting, and shows better performance based on limited evaluations settings.
The idea of using spectrograms only as part of the network (part of input to the decoder Transformer) is novel and interesting.
I appreciate that the authors used several different datasets to evaluate their model.
I also appreciate that the authors compared their method with several baselines.
weaknesses: The paper lacks a clear explanation of the clinical challenge it addresses, particularly what is meant by "idiosyncrasies" and the ambiguous phrase "this clinical challenge" in the introduction.
It is unclear why the proposed method is specifically tailored for single lead data.
There are insufficient experiments to confirm whether the proposed method accurately follows the R‑R interval.
Figure 4 closely resembles the diagram in the "Attention is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017) paper, suggesting it may need to be redrawn to differentiate it from existing works.
The proposed method appears to be merely an extension of existing MDM techniques by incorporating attention on spectrograms, raising concerns about its novelty.

Since there has been significant prior research on generating spectrograms from ECG and utilizing them alongside raw waveforms, the approach of adding spectrograms of patch-based waveforms as additional inputs in the MDM approach is not particularly novel (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.05555, https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/14/21/9936).

The paper lacks a clear explanation of how tasks were evaluated; for instance, in the case of MIT‑AFIB, it is unclear how Accuracy and F1 were calculated and what criteria were used to determine True Positives.
The ablation study does not seem to consider a sufficiently wide range of parameters, and the benchmarks used for comparison appear too weak given the performance of other methods in Table 2.
Descriptions of the figures are insufficient, with missing information about the ECG waveform and the lack of error bars in the ablation study results.
The model’s accuracy and F1 score seem insufficient, especially considering that other models for diagnosing AFib on the MIT‑BIH Arrhythmia dataset have achieved very high levels of performance.

In the benchmarking on PTB‑XL and CPSC2018, CuPID showed lower performance compared to ST‑MEM; given that ST‑MEM is applicable to both single‑lead and multi‑lead ECG, this raises questions about the utility of CuPID.
Figure 3 seems the main figure of the paper, and I’ll suggesting moving it to the first/second page. Page 5 is too late.
Formula 1 seems unnecessary and does not add much value.
[Line 262] Why spectrogram information was introduced in the second block is not well justified.
Formula 2 seems unnecessary as well, as people should generally know what L1 loss is, and it sounds common sense to not backpropagate on unmasked tokens.

[Line 310-312] There are many decisions made here without any justification; for example, the episode length, sampling frequency and patching are also important decisions which might affect performance significantly.
On top of the above, this study only considers one configuration, which is unreasonable given the relatively small size of the model.
The benchmark datasets are limited in terms of downstream tasks.
The ablation study is highly limited; for example, alternative ways of introducing the spectrogram (via Q rather than K, or concatenation instead of elementwise addition) are not explored.

Authors have not acknowledged/discussed very important related literature on modeling single‑lead ECG and masked data modeling (MDM) [1‑4]; claims that applying MDM methods to single‑lead ECG is impractical are not clearly backed by the literature.

Significant details about how the baseline models/methods were trained are missing; baseline hyperparameters differ markedly and it is unclear how they were chosen or tuned to ensure fair comparisons.

The presentation throughout the manuscript can be significantly improved; figures have inconsistent font sizes, and it is unclear whether the decoder Transformer in Figure 4 includes skip connections.
Figure 1 is adopted from other works and contains well‑known information about ECG; it may be unnecessary as a main figure and could be moved to an appendix.
Inconsistent naming for JEPA in Figure 6.
Panels b and c from Figure 2 could be combined, and Figures 2 and 3 could also be merged for better visual representation.
The details of evaluations are missing; choices of cross‑validation schemes and predictor models across datasets appear arbitrary and are not explained.
Claims in L151‑L153 are not supported; hypotheses ruling out pre‑training frameworks that do not reconstruct the signal lack theoretical or comprehensive empirical backup.
Several typos throughout the manuscript could be fixed (e.g., L149: "we consider a more suitable to", L80: missing space, L367: header in Table 1 does not match the acronym in L357).
